Tariffs I have to disagree with you on, because I'd say you're viewing the advantages of lowered prices in the background. A lower price on imported goods means more disposable income to spend on other goods. This means businesses will invest to expand their production, which means hiring more people, leading to a net increase in jobs in the economy. Sure, tariffing an imported good means higher wages, but by how much, and for whom? The businesses that are being "protected" by tariffs are the country's least competitive economic sectors, industries with relatively poor pay compared to the alternatives. A good example of this Obama's levy on Chinese tires that he put in while he was in office. The benefit for this, or so he claimed, was that 1,200 jobs were saved by this tariff. All well and good, but the consumer cost in greater expenses totaled up to over a billion dollars annually...and the average salary of those workers was 40 thousand. If imported goods are "stealing" jobs because foreign firms happen to be better at certain things, the proper course of action is to specialize--as I mentioned before, lowered prices means more incentive for businesses to grow, and the ones that will grow the most are the export sectors--the areas in which US firms are the most skilled, and provide a much better service to the international competition. Remember, although we import an awful lot, we're also the second biggest exporter in the world after China, even with only a third of the population. Yes, there will be some friction involved, as some people will have to retrain to exploit these new opportunities, but that's hardly an unsolvable issue. Industrial policy is the answer, scholarships and the like. Plenty of private firms are doing this already, because it's in their own interest to ensure that they have a steady supply of labor to meet increasing demand. In my home state, for instance, the auto firms will give scholarships to students of the local tech school, on the condition that they come work for them as engineers after graduating. Trying to prop up a noncompetitive industry with tariffs or subsidies is counterproductive, and ends up doing more harm to the economy than good.
